newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rice and radios help Sudan hostage negotiator.
newsitem.headline: Rice and radios help Sudan hostage negotiator.

text.p: U.S. congressman Bill Richardson, a personal friend of Bill Clinton, clinched his latest hostage-freeing deal sitting under a tree opposite gun-toting rebels in the middle of the African bush.
"It was very surreal," he said after securing the release of three International Committee of the Red Cross staff members after 38 days of captivity in rebel hands in south Sudan.
Richardson bargained the rebels' demand for a $100 million ransom down to five tonnes of rice, four jeeps, radios and a promised ICRC health survey in their disease-ridden camp.
"I've never negotiated in Africa for hostages. It's tough," he said. "We ended up shaking hands. It was an incredible experience."

Richardson, a Democrat of New Mexico, took Australian nurse Maree Worthington, American pilot John Early and Kenyan pilot Mohsin Raza out of the Sudanese bush to Geneva on board a U.S. military plane on Monday night.

After an emotional airport welcome by relatives with flowers and cameras, watched stoically by armed Swiss security guards, 26-year-old nurse Worthington told reporters: "I think I'll get a safer job in a nuclear reactor or something."

The three fell into the hands of militia led by Commander Kerubino Kwanyin Kol on November 1 when their plane landed at Wunrok in southern Sudan to take home five Sudanese soldier patients discharged from a Red Cross hospital in northern Kenya.

The rebels, a breakaway group of the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) which has been fighting for autonomy of the mainly Christian and animist south against Khartoum's Moslem government for 13 years, first demanded $100 million, then came down to $2.5 million.
In the end, they decided aid is better than cash.
An ICRC spokesman said the hostage deal could be a worrying precedent.
"It could set a precedent. People could start trading ICRC staff for landcruisers," said Urs Boegli.
Richardson, Clinton's special envoy on sensitive diplomatic missions, has an unusual track record of freeing hostages.

Only last week, he negotiated the release of an American held in North Korea on spying charges, the second U.S. citizen he has recovered there. He sprang two U.S. contract workers from Iraq in July 1995, and brought three political prisoners out of Cuba to the United States in February 1996.
"This was one of my toughest," he told reporters.
After a day of talks, he said he politely turned down an invitation by the rebel chief -- "a very charismatic but unpredictable man" -- to stay the night.
After this first Africa mission, Richardson said he would be ready to go on other hostage trips to the troubled continent.
Asked about his secret to success, he said: "You have to listen, you have to show respect and understand the other side's position."
The three ICRC captives lived in a mud hut, dined on goat meat and whiled away their time playing games and reading a novel sent by the ICRC on U.S. prisoners of war in Vietnam.
Pilot Early, 51, said he taught Worthington how to tell the difference between incoming and outgoing bullets when the village was attacked by rival rebels and how to play gin rummy.
Early's family called in Richardson, who visited both Khartoum and the militia-held town of Gogrial.
Early, who has worked in hotspots including Somalia, Burundi, Rwanda and Zaire, said he was not going back to Africa. "I'm getting tired of being shot at," he said.
